item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded: Both the "let me fucking die" diary entry and the drawn out commentary at the end were wholly unnecessary, and ruined what could've easily been a good -EX article. The first one is an extremely overused trope, especially on the wiki, and the second didn't add anything beyond forcing a message that I didn't need to enjoy the article down my throat in the least interesting way possible.

item.title: Yeah, I am going to no vote.
item.content:encoded:
If Kant counters are flawless anomaly detectors, then the Foundation's job is rendered basically trivial (especially since it follows that SRAs are universal neutralizers, since Kant counters are SRAs).

Realistically most anomolies investigated by the Foundation should turn out to be explicable, just due to probability. The only reason that -EX articles don't outnumber the mainlist in real life is that nobody actually wants to read thousands of fictional examples of expiremental error, unrepeatable results and hoaxes but we probably should still imagine that these articles exist in-universe. The Foundation, not being idiots, knows this, and they would have known it in 1920 too.

This was bleak in the extreme. This was extremely cold Foundation. The shift between his bored frustration during the pointless confinement to the hopeless terror at his callous discharge was well depicted.

And oh jumping catfish, the suggestion of how he died. That was like being in OGPU custody and then being handed over to the Gestapo.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
There's a lot of stuff in here I dislike; the written account given by the guy from the brewery doesn't at all feel grounded in the time period to which it belongs (it reads too forced; like someone trying to 'mimic' the style of the time-period), the interview is way too heavy-handed, the commentary at the end feels too stiff…

…but this is legitimately a great idea, and the first time I've seen an -EX that amounts to using the Foundation as a witness protection program. As much as I might complain about some of the presentation, the prose is strong, the idea excellent, and the execution — while not precisely to my liking — is still clear and sharp enough to pull an upvote out of my bitter, withered, blackened heart.

An interesting and fairly original idea, but I really disliked the reader being hammered over the head with the moral of the story at the end like a public service announcement.

Also not really comfortable with the idea that the Foundation has consistent ways to 'objectively' detect anomalies in the 21st century, unless the implication is that these continue to be unreliable (I don't object to the existence of Humes and such, but only when they're used in individual articles as a way to add to the story, not so much as something standard).

item.title: Author Post
item.content:encoded:
I got the interest in doing a Chicago Spirit article ever since reading the first 40 pages of Public Enemies: America’s Greatest Crime Wave and the Birth of the FBI, 1933-34 by Bryan Burrough, and the idea from a comment left by PeppersGhost on SCP-3036 about the idea of someone not wanting to leave the Foundation. This came from a combination of those two interests.

Thank you to Ninevolt, Peppersghost, DrChandra, Ember16, BlueBloodStains, Kakroom, and Avocadonut. Couldn't have done it without you!
